items.title: Arturo O'Farrill interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2024
items.q: And when I think of my heroes, in addition to Carla Bley and Chico O’Farrill, I think of Charles Mingus.

ctx.x: I actually created the Global Jazz Studies program first for Brooklyn College and then when I went to UCLA they already had a Global Jazz Studies program in place. So a lot of that is the realization that a lot of academia is making about the nature of jazz. In the first case we have to — this is not a popular position but I’ll go ahead and state it. Jazz is — we know this, it’s a verifiable fact — jazz is a word that was made up for a concert. It was put on a flyer and it was even denigrated — it was, I forget…

what it means to be American, which means to embrace multiplicity. The real definition of America is a nation borne out of many, many, many people. The nation was not founded by white Europeans, it was already here with indigenous beings and the indigenous people are the Americans who were already here. So the United States, the history of many people coming together to form this union. And that’s to me is what jazz is. Jazz at its best represents the multiplicity of cultures, the trans-culturation of humanity.…
Were there certain parts of the world where, let’s say the melodic contributions came from? We’ve been talking mostly about rhythm. What about the melody and the form?
